Stage 3 · Grammar

The infinitive with to

One form, four places it goes.

Read these four sentences from the recording and the text.
  • My job is to advise clients about their advertising campaigns.
  • I don’t expect to stay in this job forever.
  • It’s difficult to relax when you’re with clients.
  • She went to the meeting to explain the new system.
In which sentence does to answer the question why?
Where the infinitive goes
UsePatternExample
after some verbswant / need / hope / decide / learn / expect / offer / agree / try + to + verbI don’t expect to stay in this job forever.
after an adjectiveit’s + easy / difficult / important / nice + to + verbIt’s difficult to relax when you’re with clients.
after a noun with bemy job / my role / the plan + is + to + verbMy job is to advise clients.
to say whyto + verb = in order toShe went to the meeting to explain the system.
Negativenot + to + verb — He decided not to apply.  ·  the not comes first
The other formSome verbs take -ing, not to: enjoy, finish, mind, suggest, give up, keep. — I enjoy working from home. ✗ I enjoy to work
to + verb what comes before it

FORM. to + the plain verb. It never changes: to advise, to recruit, to be.

USE. Four places: after certain verbs, after an adjective, after a noun with be, and to say why.

NEGATIVE. not goes in front: He decided not to apply.

Not “My job is advise clients”, not “I want going home”, not “I enjoy to work”.

The -ing half of this was Unit 4 and Unit 10. Task 4 puts the two back together.

FORM. to + the plain form of the verb — to advise, to recruit, to be, to have. It does not change for the person and it does not change for the tense: I want to go, she wants to go, they wanted to go.

USE 1 — after certain verbs. want, need, hope, decide, learn, expect, offer, agree, promise, try, would like, seem. These verbs are followed by to, never by -ing.

USE 2 — after an adjective. It’s important to answer every enquiry. It’s hard to train someone you never see. The pattern is it’s + adjective + to + verb.

USE 3 — after a noun with be. This is the one this lesson is built on: My job is to… One of my main roles is to… The plan is to… Use it whenever you describe what a job involves.

USE 4 — to say why. She went to the meeting to explain the system. Here to means in order to. English does not use for + verb here.

Four mistakes to watch: “My job is advise clients” (missing to) · “I want going home” (wrong form after want) · “I enjoy to work from home” (enjoy takes -ing) · “I went there for ask about the job” (use to ask).

A short list to keep: enjoy, finish, mind, suggest, give up, keep, spend time all take -ing. Almost everything else on this page takes to.

Real sentences from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — The infinitive with to

Form

After certain verbswant · need · decide · hope · learn · agree · offer · promise + to + verb
After adjectivesIt’s important to be on time. · It’s hard to say no.
To say whyShe came to ask about the job. · I phoned to confirm the time.
After nounsthe first person to arrive · a lot of work to do
NegativeI decided not to go.

When and why we use it

  • To + verb is the normal way of answering the question why? — and it is shorter than because.
  • After It is + adjective, English uses the infinitive: It’s difficult to find a good candidate.
  • My job is to… is the standard way of describing what a role involves.
  • After make and let there is no to: They made me wait. She let me go.

Signal words

in order to · so as to · it’s important / difficult / easy to…

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • It’s important being polite. → It’s important to be polite.Infinitive after this pattern.
  • I came for ask about the job. → I came to ask about the job.To + verb says why.
  • She made me to wait. → She made me wait.No to after make.
  • My job is making the work visible. → My job is to make the work visible.Fixed pattern with the infinitive.

Don’t confuse it with

to + verb answers why?; for + noun also answers why? — but never for + verb: for a coffee, not for drink.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What changed when the office stopped being the place.

Before you read: when a team stops sharing an office, what happens to the amount of paperwork?

Decide first. The text answers this in paragraph two.

What a job involves now

Ten years ago almost nobody in Europe worked from home. Then, very quickly, millions of people had to. Today about one worker in four in the European Union is remote or hybrid — at home for part of the week, in the office for the rest. Some companies have worked this way for five years now and say they will not go back. Companies that used to measure a working day in hours try to measure it in results instead.

The job titles have not changed much, but the day-to-day work has. A manager’s first task used to be to watch the room. Now it is to write things down. “My job is to make the work visible,” says Priya Menon, who has led a hybrid team in Bengaluru since 2020. “If nobody can see you, somebody has to explain in detail what everyone is doing.” That means more paperwork, not less: reports, notes, and a short written answer to every enquiry.

Not everything is better. It is harder to train a new candidate when the team is in five places. Managers say it takes longer to recruit, and much longer to know whether the new person is any good. But productivity has not fallen. In most studies it has stayed the same or risen slightly, and workers say the same three things: they are less often in a hurry, their week is more flexible, and they are no longer in trouble for arriving ten minutes late.

One warning sits under all of this. The people who do best in a hybrid team already knew everybody before the team split up. For a new candidate, the first six months are much harder than they used to be, and no amount of paperwork fixes that.

Sources. Written for this course from public research: Eurofound, Living and working in the EU (telework series) · Eurostat, employed persons working from home · Bloom, Han & Liang (2024), Nature 630, on hybrid work and productivity. Figures are rounded. Priya Menon is a composite manager written for this course; no words are attributed to a real person.
